jsonld.name: Harira Night Cup
jsonld.description: Harira is the soup of the broken fast: every Ramadan evening in every Moroccan city, the kitchens and the charities and the cafés ladle it out at the sunset cannon's boom, and the first cup breaks the day's thirst the way no other soup on earth is asked to. It is a complete meal in a bowl — lentils, chickpeas, vermicelli, tomato, celery leaves, and lamb on the bone — thickened at the end with a flour-and-water slurry (the tedouira) and finished with a storm of cilantro and lemon. The "night cup" is its street format: served in glasses at the terrace cafés after dark, the soup that follows Moroccans from the iftar table into the evening.

A fist each of cilantro and parsley (about 50 g), half minced for the pot and half for the finish
3 celery stalks with leaves (about 100 g), the leaves minced in, one stalk diced
100 g vermicelli, added near the end

The juice of 1–2 lemons at the table; more cilantro, a pinch more cinnamon over each glass

Checkpoint: the broth should run deep red-brown and smell of the whole spice row — tomato's sweetness and the herbs' green running together. Rinse the lentils, add them to the pot with the diced celery, and simmer 10 minutes; then the vermicelli, stirring so it separates, 4 minutes more, until both are just tender. Harira Night Cup

Moroccan · Medium · Serves 6

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
Harira is the soup of the broken fast: every Ramadan evening in every Moroccan city, the kitchens and the charities and the cafés ladle it out at the sunset cannon's boom, and the first cup breaks the day's thirst the way no other soup on earth is asked to. It is a complete meal in a bowl — lentils, chickpeas, vermicelli, tomato, celery leaves, and lamb on the bone — thickened at the end with a flour-and-water slurry (the tedouira) and finished with a storm of cilantro and lemon. The "night cup" is its street format: served in glasses at the terrace cafés after dark, the soup that follows Moroccans from the iftar table into the evening.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

The base

The tedouira (the thickener)

  • and, the purists' addition, a spoon of the #100 matbucha or a fresh tomato blended in
- **Soak the chickpeas the full 8 hours.** Harira's chickpeas must arrive whole and tender in a soup whose other elements run to softness — an under-soaked chickpea is a pebble in the glass, and the soup's whole clock is built around their tenderness. - **The bridge:** celery leaves are the soup's green signature and run under-bought — they are the same bunch's tops, saved. The lamb bridges to beef on the bone or is honestly omitted for the Lenten vegetarian version (add a smoked paprika whisper for depth).

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • The base: chickpeas whole-tender, broth deep, under-salted by design.
  • The clocks: lentils 10, vermicelli 4 — timed and no more.
  • The tedouira: streamed thin, stirred one direction, gloss like velvet.

Harira Night Cup

Prep: 30 minutes, plus 8 hours soaking · Cook: 1 hour 20 minutes · Total: About 9 hours 50 minutes (mostly soaking) · Serves 6

Ingredients

The base

  • 200 g lamb on the bone (shank or neck pieces), cut small
  • 100 g dried chickpeas, soaked 8 hours; 100 g dried brown lentils
  • 2 tbsp neutral oil; 1 onion (about 150 g), minced fine
  • 1 can (400 g) tomatoes, crushed, or 600 g fresh grated; 2 tbsp tomato paste (about 30 g)
  • 4 cloves garlic (about 15 g), grated; 1 tsp each ginger and turmeric; ½ tsp black pepper; 1 tsp cumin; ½ tsp cinnamon (the soup's quiet register)
  • A fist each of cilantro and parsley (about 50 g), half minced for the pot and half for the finish
  • 3 celery stalks with leaves (about 100 g), the leaves minced in, one stalk diced
  • 1.8 litres water; 2 tsp salt
  • 100 g vermicelli, added near the end

The tedouira (the thickener)

  • 4 tbsp flour (about 35 g) whisked smooth with 250 ml water — and, the purists' addition, a spoon of the #100 matbucha or a fresh tomato blended in
  • The juice of 1–2 lemons at the table; more cilantro, a pinch more cinnamon over each glass

Instructions

  1. **The long base (50 minutes).** Brown the lamb lightly in the oil over medium — the oil at about 150 °C — add the onion, garlic, spices, and tomato paste, and fry 3 minutes; add the tomatoes, drained chickpeas, water, the minced herb fist, and the celery — bring to a bare simmer, cover ajar, and cook 45 minutes, until the chickpeas are nearly tender. Checkpoint — the broth should run deep red-brown and smell of the whole spice row — tomato's sweetness and the herbs' green running together. Taste: one notch under-salted, one notch under-thick — both corrections come at the end.
  2. **The lentils and vermicelli (15 minutes).** Rinse the lentils, add them to the pot with the diced celery, and simmer 10 minutes; then the vermicelli, stirring so it separates, 4 minutes more, until both are just tender. Checkpoint — the lentils should be intact but yielding, the vermicelli al dente — both cook quickly and both turn to mush past their clock, so the last two additions are timed, not watched casually.
  3. **The tedouira (10 minutes of stirring — the soup's craft).** Whisk the flour smooth with its water (no lumps — a shaker or a blender's ten seconds), bring the soup to a steady bubble, and pour the slurry in a thin stream while stirring constantly in one direction. The soup thickens over the next 5 minutes of stirring to a glossy, coat-the-glass velvet. Off the heat: the remaining cilantro, salt to final taste. Checkpoint — the finished harira should coat a spoon in a slow film and hold the vermicelli suspended — thick enough to stand a bread's dunk, thin enough to drink from a glass. The tedouira's stirring is not optional: an unstirred slurry cooks to dumplings, and the glossy velvet is the soup's identity.
  4. **Serve in glasses or bowls — with the full finish.** Each glass: a hard squeeze of lemon, a pinch of the reserved cilantro, a whisper of cinnamon over the surface, and the dates and chebakia on the side in the Ramadan tradition. Checkpoint — eating test: the first swallow is the soup's whole job — lemon-bright, tomato-deep, the lamb's savor and the herbs' green, thick enough to feel like food and hot enough to break a fast — then the textures arrive: a chickpea here, a lentil there, the vermicelli's silk. It should taste like evening and abundance, and the second glass is the tradition.

Finish & Plate

Glasses or small bowls, the lemon and cilantro at the table, cinnamon whispered over each — dates and the sesame sweets beside in the Ramadan format, bread for the dunking in the everyday one.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Soup dull, flatLemon or cilantro short at the finishBoth are structural \u2014 pour generously
Tedouira lumpySlurry un-whisked or un-stirredBlend it smooth; the one-direction stir
Lentils, vermicelli mushyAdded too earlyThe timed additions at the end only

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- The base (through step 1) keeps 3 days refrigerated or freezes 2 months — the harira station; the lentils, vermicelli, and tedouira are always fresh per pot. The finished soup thickens overnight — re-thin with water and re-finish with lemon. - Variations: the beef-bone version, the vegetarian's smoked-paprika depth. The #18 lablabi and the #7 bessara are harira's fellow dawn-and-dusk soups on this site — three nations' liquid bread.
